title: The Nines
full_review:
In his screenplay for "The Nines" (Newmarket), writer-director John August sets himself, his cast and his audience quite a challenge. As it spins a single, unified but complex tale through the telling of three different stories, his script takes nothing for granted and respects its audience enough to give them, for the most part, only clues, not explanations.

In addition to keeping the viewer's attention, this sophisticated approach to storytelling also elicits some outstanding performances from the film's three principal actors. Each is called upon to portray a series of three characters who are subtly different, yet intriguingly the same.

As -- successively -- a TV star, a television writer and a video-game designer, the male protagonist (Ryan Reynolds) is consistently perturbed and uncertain about the border between reality and illusion. At his side in each story are two female protagonists (Melissa McCarthy and Hope Davis). Each offers him guidance, but their advice is always contradictory, as are their interests and goals.

All three actors impressively rise to the challenge the film poses for them. Reynolds, for instance, moves ably between his first character, an aggressively heterosexual heartthrob and his second, a gay man whom he portrays without a hint of caricature.

The members of the supporting cast (Elle Fanning, David Denman and Octavia Spenser), whose task is to witness the central drama from a variety of different perspectives, are equally strong.

However, despite its originality and the fine acting with which it is brought to life, "The Nines" suffers from some serious flaws. The most significant of these is the metaphysical baggage with which the story is loaded down.

In his effort to examine the nature of both divine and human creativity, August establishes his own mythological system within the film. This requires the cast to engage in lengthy explanations, which slow the film's otherwise quick pace. This aspect of the story also distances the characters from the audience and weakens the bond of shared experience between them.

This is one reason why an earlier film with which "The Nines" has some thematic similarities -- 1990's "Jacob's Ladder" -- has a much deeper and more lasting impact.

Where the older film dealt so deftly in illusion and doubt, the newer one labors to create its alternate universe, or at least a rival perception of reality.

August's conceit, in addition to being cumbersome, also leads to some ill-considered, irreligious jokes and even to a possible questioning of the existence of God. This ultimate issue, however, remains unresolved by the movie's conclusion.

"The Nines" takes some admirable risks, and most of these pay off. Unfortunately, the film also engages in the aforementioned woolgathering, from which it profits nothing.

The film contains sexual activity, some of it adulterous; much rough, crude and crass language; two instances of profanity; irresponsible drinking; drug use; prostitution; and irreverent speech and behavior. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted. Under 17 requires accompanying parent or adult guardian.
